1.7.m: Bhīṣma said: / How were the Maruts, beloved of the gods, born as sons of Diti? / And why did they enter into matchless friendship with their co-wives' sons, the gods?
Pulastya said: / Formerly, when the Asuras were slain by Hari in the war between gods and Asuras, / [Diti,] stricken with grief over her sons and grandsons, went to the supreme earthly realm.
At the great holy site in Puṣkara, on the auspicious bank of the Sarasvatī, / intent on worshipping her husband, she performed fierce austerities.
Indeed, Diti, the mother of the Daityas, faithful to her vows, engaged in the work of the sages; / subsisting on fruit, she performed austerities with the kṛcchra, cāndrāyana, and other penances.
For more than a full hundred years, she was overcome by old age and grief; / then, burning with austerities, she questioned Vasiṣṭha and other [sages]:
“Please tell me of a vow that destroys grief for one's sons, / that yields the fruit of good fortune, both in this world and in the next.”
Vasiṣṭha and the other [sages] told of the vow of the full moon of Jyeṣṭha, / by whose grace she became free from grief for her sons.
Bhīṣma said: / O brāhmaṇa, I wish to hear of the vow of the full moon of Jyeṣṭha, / by which Diti obtained forty-nine sons once again.
Pulastya said: / The vow that was previously described to Diti by Vasiṣṭha and others— / hear that very [vow] from me in detail.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, during the bright fortnight, on the full moon day, observing the vow, / one should place a flawless jar filled with white rice,
furnished with various fruits, likewise provided with stalks of sugar cane, / covered with a pair of white garments, and smeared with white sandalwood paste,
accompanied by various foods to eat, and with gold according to one's means. / Above that, one should place a copper vessel accompanied by molasses.
Above that, one should make a golden Brahmā inside the hollow of a lotus, / and on his left side, Sāvitrī accompanied by sugar.
One should offer fragrance and incense to both, and have song and instrumental music performed. / If that is lacking, how should one perform it? As the Grandfather on a lotus:
Having fashioned an auspicious image named Brahmā made of molasses, / one should worship the lotus-born [deity] with white flowers, unbroken rice grains, and sesame seeds.

[Saying,] “To the one endowed with Brahman,” having worshipped both feet, and the two shanks [saying,] “To the giver of good fortune”; / the two thighs [saying,] “To Viriñci,” and the waist saying, “To Manmatha”;

the belly [saying,] “To the one with a pure belly,” the chest of the Creator saying, “To the unwearied”; / the face [saying,] “To the lotus-faced,” and the two arms to the one whose hands hold the Vedas;
[saying,] “Homage to the Universal Self,” one should worship the crown of the head, and also the lotus. / Then, at dawn, one should offer that jar to a brāhmaṇa.
One should feed a brāhmaṇa with devotion, while oneself eating without salt; / with devotion one should make a clockwise circumambulation and utter this mantra:
“May the Lord, the Grandfather of all the worlds, be pleased here— / he who is called the bliss in the heart of all the worlds!”
Following this procedure, one should perform everything month by month; / fasting on the full moon day, one should worship the imperishable Brahmā.
Consuming only a single fruit, one should sleep at night on the ground. / Then, in the thirteenth month, accompanied by a cow made of clarified butter,
one should give to Viriñci a bed endowed with all household utensils; / having made Brahmā out of gold, and likewise Sāvitrī out of silver,
the lotus-natured Creator of the universe, having attained Sāvitrī. / Having worshipped with garments and ornaments a twice-born together with his wife in devotion,
one should give cows and other [gifts] according to one's capacity, and say: “May he be pleased!” / One should perform a fire oblation with white sesame seeds and chant the names of Brahmā.
Likewise with bovine clarified butter and with milk-rice, O knower of dharma. / Then one should give wealth to the vipras, and garlands of flowers according to one's means.
Whoever performs this according to the rule on the full moon day, or even women, / freed from all sins, attains absorption into Brahman.
In this world, such a one unfailingly enjoys excellent sons and good fortune. / He who is Brahmā is remembered as Viṣṇu, the blissful Maheśvara.
One who desires happiness should remember the god, the Grandfather, in whichever form he desires. / Having heard thus, that Diti performed everything in its entirety.
Through the power of the vow, Kaśyapa arrived in supreme joy; / her who had become harsh, he made once more endowed with beauty and charm.
He gratified her with boons, and she chose the best of boons: / “A son capable of slaying Śakra and possessed of great splendor,
a great-souled one who will destroy all the immortals, I choose as a boon.” / Kaśyapa spoke these words: “A mighty slayer of Indra
I will grant through this; however, O auspicious one, let this be done: / Having performed the sacrifice of Āpastamba for the sake of a son today, O woman of beautiful breasts,
I will then produce an embryo after touching both your auspicious breasts. / There will be an auspicious embryo, O goddess, a slayer of Śakra.”
Then he performed the sacrifice for obtaining a son according to Āpastamba, rich in wealth; / saying, “Become the enemy of Indra,” he offered the oblations in haste.
The gods were bewildered, the Daityas turned away, and so did the Dānavas. / Then Kaśyapa placed the embryo into Diti and spoke to her again:
“Your face resembles the moon, your two breasts are like bilva fruits, / your lips have the shape of coral, and your complexion is exceedingly radiant.
Seeing you, O large-eyed woman, I forget my own body. / Therefore, O fair-hipped one, the embryo has been sown by my hand upon your breasts.
Great effort must be made by you regarding this embryo, O fair-faced woman; / live for one hundred years in this penance grove.
At twilight, a pregnant woman must never eat, O woman of excellent complexion; / she must never stand nor go near the roots of trees at any time.
She should not sit on implements such as pestles and mortars; / she must not plunge into deep water, and should avoid an empty house.
She should not stand on anthills, nor become agitated in mind; / she must not scratch the earth with her nails, nor with charcoal or ashes.
She should not constantly be lying down, and must avoid physical exertion; / she should not sit on chaff, charcoal, ashes, bones, or skull-fragments.
She should avoid quarrelling with people, and likewise rubbing her limbs [with oil]; / she should not stand with dishevelled hair, nor ever become impure.
She should not sleep with her head pointing north, nor ever with her head pointing downward; / as a virtuous wife, she should not be without clothes, nor agitated, nor with wet feet.
She should not speak inauspicious words, nor indulge in excessive laughter; / she should constantly perform worship along with elders, intent on auspiciousness.
She should bathe with water infused with all medicinal herbs; / protected by rites, she should be devoted to service and respectful address.
She should remain with a cheerful face, devoted to the beloved welfare of her husband; / and she must never reproach her husband in any condition whatsoever.
"I have become emaciated and weak, and old age has come upon me; / my breasts have sagged from their place, and my face is wrinkled and lined.
You have made me like this"—she should never say such things. / "May you be well; I shall go." Being told "So be it" by her once more,
he vanished right there while all creatures were watching. / Then she observed [the vow] according to the rule declared in her husband's words.
Now Indra also, having learned of that, came to Diti's side; / abandoning the abode of the gods, he stayed there, eager to attend upon her.
Pākaśāsana was intent on seeking a lapse on Diti's part; / he was contrary and agitated within, but gracious-faced externally.
Pretending not to know that purpose of hers, while performing auspicious deeds for himself; / then, at the end of a hundred years, when it was short by only three days,
she considered herself to have accomplished her purpose, her mind astonished with joy. / Without washing her feet, lying down with her hair unbound,
overcome with heavy sleep, in the daytime, her head placed on another [unclean spot] / then, having found that opening, entering inside, the lord of Śacī,
the lord of the thirty [gods] split that embryo into seven parts with his thunderbolt. / Then those seven boys, radiant as the sun, were born.
As those seven boys were crying, they were forbidden by the enemy of the Dānavas. / As they cried yet again, Hari, with the thunderbolt in his hand,
cut each one of them into seven pieces as they remained in the womb. / Becoming forty-nine in this way, they wept exceedingly.
Indra stopped them again and again, [saying,] "Do not weep!" / Then the slayer of Vṛtra pondered with this reflection:
"By the greatness of what act have these been brought back to life again? / Having understood that this is the fruit of the full-moon [observance] through the conjunction of merit,
surely this has reached fruition, or else it is from the worship of Brahmā / that, struck by the thunderbolt, they have not met with destruction.
Because concealing the womb brought multiplicity even from one, / these are surely invulnerable; therefore let them become gods.
Since they, born from the womb, were told 'Do not weep' (mā ruda) while crying, / let them become partakers of happiness by that name: the Maruts."
Then, appeasing Diti again, saying, "Forgive me, / relying on the science of statecraft, this evil deed was committed by me,"
and having made the host of Maruts equal to the gods, the lord of the immortals / placed Diti on a celestial chariot and went to heaven along with her sons.
Then all those Maruts became enjoyers of sacrificial shares; / they did not join in unity with the Asuras, and therefore they are dear to the gods.
Bhīṣma said: / The primal creation has been told to me by you at length, O Brahman; / and tell me of the secondary creation, and who the lords over them are.
Pulastya said: / When Pṛthu was consecrated over the entire kingdom and became the master of the earth, / then he made Soma the ruler of herbs, of sacrifices, vows, and austerities,

and of constellations, stars, twice-born [birds and priests], trees, shrubs, and spreading creepers, having gold within; / likewise Varuṇa the lord of the waters, and Vaiśravaṇa the lord of riches and of kings.
He made Viṣṇu the lord of the solar deities, and Agni [the lord] of the Vasus and lord of the world; / he made Dakṣa the ruler of the Prajāpatis, and Śakra the ruler of the Maruts;

[He appointed] Prahlāda as lord of the Daitya rulers and of the Dānavas, Yama of the ancestors,
and the trident-handed [Śiva] as king of piśācas, rākṣasas, beasts, spirits, yakṣas, and vetālas.
and the snowy mountain the master of mountains, the lord ocean the ruler of rivers; / and further he made Citraratha the master of Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and Kinnaras.
He appointed Vāsuki of fierce valor the ruler of Nāgas, and Takṣaka the ruler of snakes; / he made the king of elephants named Airāvaṇa the lord of the elephants of the directions;
Suparṇa the master of birds, and Uccaiḥśravas the king of horses; / the lion [the king] of wild animals, the bull of cattle, and the plakṣa tree of all lordly trees.

Then the Grandfather had previously consecrated these, and further the protectors of all the directions: / in the eastern quarter he consecrated the guardian of the direction named Suvarman, whose banner is against foes;
then in the south he made the sovereign lord named Śaṅkhapada the ruler; / the womb of the cosmic egg made the lord Ketumant the ruler of the western direction;
he made Hiraṇyaroman, the Prajāpati and son of Megha, the ruler of the northern direction. / Even today the rulers of the directions, constantly bearing [their charge], protect the earth.

By these four was the king named Pṛthu consecrated as the first on earth; / when the [manvantara] named Cākṣuṣa had passed, they appointed this Vaivasvata on the earth.

When the [period] named Cākṣuṣa had passed and the one called Vaivasvata commenced again, / he, born of the solar lineage and bearing the marks, became the Prajāpati of this moving and unmoving [creation].
Pulastya said: / All the manvantaras, the deeds of the Manus, / the measure of a kalpa, and its creation in brief—
listen with single-minded attention and a tranquil mind, O joy of the Kurus! / Formerly, in the Svāyambhuva manvantara, there were the gods named Yāmas.
There were just seven sages remembered formerly, beginning with Marīci. / Āgnīdhra, Agnibāhu, Vibhu, and Savana,
Jyotiṣmant, Dyutimant, Bhavya, Medhā, Medhātithi, and Vasu— / these ten were the increasers of the lineage of this Manu Svāyambhuva.
Having brought about the secondary creation, they went to the supreme abode. / Thus the Svāyambhuva [manvantara] has been declared; hereafter [listen to] the Svārociṣa.
The sons of Svārociṣa were four, endowed with divine splendor: / Nabhas, Nabhasya and others, Bhāvana, and Kīrtivardhana.
Datta, Agni, Cyavana, Stambha, Prāṇa, Kaśyapa, / Arvan, and Bṛhaspati—these seven were the seven sages.
Then the gods were remembered as Tuṣitas in the Svārociṣa manvantara: / Havīndra, Sukṛta, Mūrti, Āpa, and Jyotiratha are remembered [among them].
The seven sons of Vasiṣṭha who were then the Prajāpatis— / this second manvantara has been told; hereafter [hear of the next].
And I shall tell of another auspicious manvantara as well: / there the Manu named Auttami fathered ten sons:
Iṣa, Ūrja, Tanūja, Śuci, and Śukra, / Madhu, Mādhava, Nabhasya, and Nabhas,
Sahas, and Sahasya; among them Uttama was the increaser of fame. / The Bhānus were the gods there, and the Ūrjas were recorded as the seven sages:
Kaukabhiṇḍi, Kutuṇḍa, Dālbhya, Śaṅkha, Pravāhita, / Miti, and Saṃmiti—these seven were the increasers of yoga.
The fourth manvantara is renowned by the name Tāmasa: / Kapi, Pṛthu, Agni, Akapi, Kavi,
likewise Janya and Dhāman—these were the seven sages by name. / And the Sādhyas were the hosts of gods declared in the Tāmasa manvantara.
Akalmaṣa, Tapodhanvin, Tapomūla, Tapodhana, / Taporāśi, Tapasya, Sutapasya, and Paraṃtapa—
all these ten sons of Tāmasa were increasers of the lineage. / Likewise, hear about the manvantara of the fifth Manu, Raivata:
Devabāhu, Subāhu, Parjanya, the sage Samaya, / Hiraṇyaroman, and Saptāśva—these seven were remembered as the sages.
The gods and the Bhūtarajasas are traditionally known as the Prakṛtis: / Avaśa, Tattvadarśin, Vītimat, Havyapa, Kapi,
Mukta, Nirutsuka, Sattva, Nirmoha, and Prakāśaka. / Endowed with the strength of dharma and valor, these ten are the sons of Revata.

Bhṛgu, Sudhāman, Virajas, Sahiṣṇu, Nārada,
Vivasvat, and Kṛti by name—these are the other seven sages.

In the Cākṣuṣa [manvantara], the gods were celebrated by the name of Lekhas;
and Vibhava and Pṛthak are declared as heaven-dwellers.

When the period of Cākṣuṣa arrived, there were five classes of gods;
likewise Ruru and the others were the ten sons of Cākṣuṣa,

Who were spoken of to you by me previously in the Svāyambhuva lineage.
Thus the Cākṣuṣa manvantara has been recounted by me to you.

And I will speak of the seventh, which is called Vaivasvata:
Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, Gautama,

Bhāradvāja, the yogin Viśvāmitra of great majesty,
and Jamadagni—these seven are now the great sages.

Having established the order of dharma, they depart to the supreme state.
I shall [now] declare the future period of Manu Sāvarṇya.

Aśvatthāman, Śaradvant, Kauśika, Gālava,
Śatānanda, Kāśyapa, and Rāma are remembered as the sages.

Dhṛti, Varīyas, Yavasu, Suvarṇa, and Dhṛti,
Variṣṇuvīrya, Sumati, Vasu, and mighty Śukra—

These are proclaimed as the sons of the future Manu Arka-sāvarṇi.
Raucya and the other Manus are also proclaimed.

The son of the Prajāpati Ruci will be named Raucya;
likewise the Manu who is the son of Bhūti will be named Bhautya.

Thereafter, Merusāvarṇi, the son of Brahmā, is remembered as Manu,
as well as Ṛbhu, Ṛtudhāman, and Manu Viṣvaksena.

Thus the past and future Manus have been celebrated.
A thousand yugas of years are spanned by them, O king.

Having brought forth all this moving and unmoving [creation] in their respective periods,
they are liberated together with Brahmā at the end of the kalpa, when their duties cease.

1.8.m:
Bhīṣma said:
It is heard that of old the earth was enjoyed by many rulers of the earth.
Kings are called *pārthivas* from connection with *pṛthivī* (the earth); from whose connection is the earth [called] *pṛthivī*?

And for what reason was that conventional name given to the earth?
Or why is this name "Gauḥ" (the cow) [applied] to the earth? Tell me!

Pulastya said:
Formerly, in the Kṛta age, there was a Prajāpati named Aṅga.
By him the very foul-faced daughter of Mṛtyu was taken as wife.

Sunīthā was her name, and her son of old was named Vena:
devoted to adharma, lustful, mighty, a ruler of the earth,

Doing adharma to the world, and an abductor of others' wives.
Then, for his purification and for the welfare of the world, by the great sages,

Though entreated, that impure-souled one did not grant safety.
Then, having slain him with a curse, distressed by the fear of kinglessness,

The sinless brāhmaṇas churned his body by force.
From that body being churned, the tribes of Mlecchas were produced,

Shining like black collyrium, through the portion of the mother in the body.
Through association with the portion of the father, a righteous and law-abiding

Son arose from his right hand, bearing bow, arrows, and mace,
composed of divine splendour, wearing jewelled armor and armlets.

He became Pṛthu by name, and he was Viṣṇu born.
Having been consecrated by the brāhmaṇas and having performed very difficult austerities,

The lord attained sovereignty over everything through the boon of Viṣṇu.
Beholding the surface of the earth devoid of Vedic recitation and the *vaṣaṭ* exclamation, devoid of dharma,

He of immeasurable valour was intent upon piercing it in anger with an arrow.
Then, assuming the form of a cow, the earth sought to flee.

Pṛthu, with arrow and bow, pursued behind her.
Then, standing in one place, she said: "What shall I do?"

Pṛthu also spoke the word: "Grant the desired [nourishment], O virtuous one,
quickly for all the world, both stationary and moving!"

The earth said, "So be it!" and that king milked [her]
into his own hand, making Manu Svāyambhuva the calf.

That milk became the food by which creatures live.
Then she was milked by the sages; Soma was then the calf,

Vācaspati was the milker, the Veda was the vessel, and ascetic power was the fluid.
And the earth was milked by the gods; the Wind-god was then the milker,

Indra became the calf, the milk was powerful strength,
and the vessel of the gods was gold, and [that] of the ancestors was silver.

Antaka was the milker, Yama was the calf, and *svadhā* was the fluid;
a hole was the vessel of the serpent-spirits, and Takṣaka was the calf.

Poison was the milk, and Dhṛtarāṣṭra was the milker.
She was also milked by the Asuras into an iron [vessel], [milking] affliction of enemies;

The vessel was illusion, the calf was Virocana son of Prahlāda,
and Trimūrdhan was the milker there, by whom illusion was set in motion.

And the earth was milked of old by the Yakṣas desiring disappearance,
making Viśvāvasu the calf, into a jewelled vessel, O king.

She was milked by the hosts of Pretas and Rakṣases of thick fat and blood;
Raupyanābha was the milker, and Sumālin was the calf.

The earth was milked again by the Gandharvas and hosts of Apsarases,
making Citraratha the calf, [milking] perfumes onto a lotus petal;

The milker was named Vasuruci, who had mastered the Atharvaveda.
The earth was milked by the mountains of various gems

And divine medicinal herbs; the mountain Meru was the milker,
Himavat was the calf there, and the vessel was made of rock.

And the earth was milked by the trees of the sap that causes sprouting when cut;
in a palāśa vessel the milker was the sāl tree full of flowering groves,

And the plakṣa tree, lord of all trees and forests, became the calf.
Thus the earth was likewise milked by others according to their desire.

There was long life, wealth, and sweet happiness while Pṛthu was ruling the kingdom:
there was no poverty, no disease, no lack of wealth, and no one committing sin;

No portents and no afflictions while Pṛthu was ruling the kingdom;
people were perpetually joyful, free from sorrow and grief.

And with the tip of his bow, having pushed aside the greatest mountains, that mighty one
made the earth's surface level, desiring the welfare of living beings.

There were no cities, villages, or forts, and men did not bear weapons;
where [people] did not die in sorrow, and there was no heed given to the *arthaśāstra*.

Men were wholly devoted to dharma while Pṛthu was ruling the kingdom.
The vessels and whatever milk [was drawn] have been told to you in this way,

According as each had a taste for something, that was granted to them by him who knew;
in all the splendours of sacrifice, all has been made known by me to you.

Because the earth attained the status of daughter to Pṛthu, O wise one,
and through the connection of following him, she is celebrated as *pṛthivī* by the wise.

Bhīṣma said:
Declare the entire solar lineage in due order, O brāhmaṇa,
and, O knower of truth, you ought to speak properly of the lunar lineage.

Rājñī, daughter of Raivata, gave birth to a son, Revata;
Prabhā gave birth to Prabhāta; and Saṃjñā, daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ, gave birth to Manu.
And Yama and Yamunā were born as twins. / Then, unable to endure the fiery form of Vivasvat,
the flawless, passionate woman, the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ, / produced from her own body a woman resembling her own form, named Chāyā.
She stood before her and said, "What shall I do?" / [Saṃjñā] spoke to her: "O fair-faced woman, attend upon that husband of mine;
protect my children with a mother's affection." / Saying "So be it," the virtuous woman departed, [yielding] the god to desire.
The god too desired her with respect, thinking, "This is Saṃjñā." / She gave birth to Sāvarṇi Manu, who had the nature of a Manu,
and [he was called] Sāvarṇi because he was of equal color (savarṇa) with Manu Vaivasvata. / Then, in due course, [he fathered upon Chāyā] a daughter, Tapatī, and a Tvaṣṭrī,
for the Sun fathered [them] on Chāyā, thinking, "This is Saṃjñā." / Then Chāyā showed greater affection for her own son, Manu.
The elder Manu did not tolerate it, and then Yama, overcome with anger, / threatened her, raising his right foot.
And Chāyā cursed Yama: "Let this one foot / be infested with worms, flowing with pus and blood!"
Overcome by the curse, Yama reported to his father: / "O lord, I was cursed without cause by my mother in her anger.
Out of childishness my foot was slightly raised once; / though restrained by Manu, she gave me a curse, O lord.
Probably she is not our mother, since she is unequal in affection." / The god spoke to Yama once again: "What can I do, O wise one?
From happiness, whose sorrow might not arise? Or rather, the sequence of karma / cannot be averted even for Śiva—what to say of other beings?
A cock will eat the worms from that foot of yours, / and this foot of yours will become lame yet handsome."
Thus addressed and comforted, he performed severe austerity / out of detachment at the sacred site Puṣkara, subsisting on fruit, water-foam, and air.
Having worshiped the Grandfather for ten thousand years, / the lord of the gods, the Lotus-born, was pleased by the power of his austerity.
He chose the status of a world protector, and the imperishable realm of the ancestors, / and the examination of this world consisting of dharma and adharma.
Thus he attained the status of a world protector from the Lotus-born, / and sovereignty over the ancestors, and over dharma and adharma, O sinless one.
Then, learning of that behavior and deed of Saṃjñā, / Vivasvat went near Tvaṣṭṛ and, full of wrath, spoke to him.
Then Tvaṣṭṛ spoke this soothing word to him: / "Unable to bear your intense brilliance, O dispeller of darkness, O lord,
assuming the form of a mare, she came here into my presence. / And she was turned away by me, O lord of heaven, out of fear of you,
[saying:] 'Since you have come here into my presence without your husband's knowledge, / therefore it is not fitting for you to enter my house.'
Thus addressed, the flawless woman quickly went to the desert region, / and assuming the form of a mare, she dwells on the surface of the earth.
Therefore grant me your favor if I am worthy of grace. / Placing you upon a machine, the Sun, I will pare away your brilliance.
I will make your form bring delight to the worlds, O lord." / Thus addressed by the Sun, he placed the Sun upon a lathe
and trimmed away his brilliance, fashioning the discus of Viṣṇu, / the trident of Rudra, and another weapon, the thunderbolt of Indra,

And Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned a great, peerless form,
which was the destroyer of the Daityas and Dānavas and consisted of a thousand rays, except for the feet.
And he was unable to look upon that form of the Sun's feet again; / therefore, even today, no one ever causes feet to be made [for him].
Whoever does so is most wicked and attains a censured destiny; / he contracts the leprosy disease called sorrow in this world.
Therefore, one who desires dharma, pleasure, and wealth / should never cause the feet of the wise god of gods to be made in paintings or temples.
Then that lord, the sovereign of the immortals, the Sun, / went to the mortal world and, stricken with desire, mated via the mouth
in the form of a horse endowed with great brilliance. / And Saṃjñā in her mind was agitated, bewildered with fear;
fearing that he was another, it was discharged through her two nostrils. / Then from his semen the two Aśvins were born, so we have heard.
They were born as Dasras from hearing, and as Nāsatyas from the tip of the nose. / Recognizing that god after a long time, she felt supreme joy.
He went to heaven in a celestial chariot together with his wife, filled with joy. / Sāvarṇi Manu also performs austerity on Mount Meru even today.
And Śani, through the power of austerity, attained equality with the planets. / Yamunā and Tapatī became rivers once again.
Likewise, the terrible Viṣṭi was established as a division of time. / And Manu Vaivasvata had ten sons of great strength:
Ila was the first of them, who was fashioned through a sacrifice for a son; / Ikṣvāku, Kuśanābha, Ariṣṭa, and Dhṛṣṭa;
Nariṣyanta, Karūṣa, the very mighty Śaryāti, / Pṛṣadhra, and Nābhāga—they were all divine humans.
Having first consecrated his righteous son Ila, / Manu went again to perform austerity at the penance-grove of Puṣkara.
Then Brahmā, the grantor of boons, came to him to grant success: / "Choose a boon as you desire, O son of Manu, good fortune to you!"
He then spoke to the lotus-eyed, lotus-born, all-pervading god: / "May all the kings on earth in my lineage, endowed with dharma,
be rulers, O Lord, by your favor, O Lotus-born!" / Having said "So be it," the lord of gods vanished right there.
Then, having returned to Ayodhyā, he resided as before. / Now once, Ila, the own son of Manu, mounted upon a chariot,
set forth to achieve his purpose across this earth filled with kings, / wandering to all the continents, subduing the monarchs.
Drawn along, the glorious king went to a pleasure-grove of Śambhu / filled with wish-fulfilling trees and creepers, the great Śaravaṇa by name,
where the lord of gods, Soma, crested with the crescent moon, takes his pleasure. / There in the Śaravaṇa an agreement had previously been made with Umā:
"Whatever has the designation of a masculine name that comes to our forest / shall all become female within a circumference of ten yojanas."
King Ila, unaware of the agreement, entered the Śaravaṇa; / instantly he became female, and in a moment the horse became a mare.
Everything done in his manhood was forgotten in the female body; / he became a woman named Ilā, with plump, prominent, firm breasts,
with elevated hips and loins, eyes long like lotus petals, / a face like the full moon, slender, coquettish, with dark eyes,
with full, elevated, long arms, dark, curly hair, / fine body hair, a lovely face, and speaking soft, stammering words,
a maiden with a fair complexion, fine, copper-colored nail-sprouts, / possessed of a pair of bow-like brows, moving with the gait of a swan.
Wandering in that forest, the passionate woman thought: / "Who might be my father here, or my brother, or who my protector?
To which husband was I given? How many years [old] am I on the earth?" / And as she was wondering, the woman was seen by the son of Soma.
His mind captivated by the form of Ilā, the woman of excellent complexion, / Budha, stricken with desire, made an effort to win her.
He assumed a distinguished appearance: tonsured, with water pot and manuscript, / garbed with a bamboo staff, wearing a sacred thread, and holding a small hoe.
In the form of a twice-born, with a topknot, reciting the Veda, wearing earrings, / accompanied by students seeking instruction, carrying kindling, flowers, kuśa grass, and water,
seeking her at that moment, he called out to virtuous Ilā, / concealed in the bower of trees outside the forest.
Agitated, he suddenly said as if in reproach: / 'Leaving the attendance of the agnihotra, where have you gone from my house?
This hour of your diversion is now passing away. / Come, come, broad-hipped lady! Why are you bewildered?
This evening hour has arrived here for dalliance. / Having smeared [the floor with cow dung], adorn my house with flowers.'
She said: 'I have forgotten everything, O ascetic! / Tell me who I am, and who you are, my husband, and what my family is, O sinless one!'
Budha said to that slender lady: 'You are Ilā, a fair-complexioned woman; / and I am a lover named Budha, known as possessing manifold learning.
Born in the family of the radiant one, my father is the lord of brāhmaṇas.' / Thus, upon his word, she entered Budha's dwelling,
which was filled with jewelled pillars and fashioned by divine power. / Remaining in that palace, Ilā considered herself fulfilled:
'Oh, what conduct! Oh, what beauty! Oh, what wealth! Oh, what lineage! / And oh, what supreme loveliness of myself and of this husband of mine!'
And she sported with him for a long time in the Ilāvṛta forest, / in that mansion full of every delight, just as in the abode of Indra.
Then his brothers, the sons of Manu, led by Ikṣvāku, / searching for the king, came near the grove of reeds.
There they all saw a mare standing before them, / peerless, shining with rays from the fringe of jewels [on her adornments].
Having arrived and recognized it, they were all filled with amazement: / 'This steed named Candraprabha belongs to that great-souled king.
For what reason has he assumed the excellent form of a mare?' / Then they questioned their family priest, the son of Mitrāvaruṇa:
'What strange event is this? Tell us, O best of those who know yoga!' / Vasiṣṭha also, seeing it with the eye of meditation, related everything:
'A stipulation was formerly made by Śambhu's beloved in the grove of reeds: / whatever male enters here shall attain the state of womanhood.
This horse too went into the state of a female along with the king. / [Now] that Ila, who is equal to the lord of wealth, may attain manhood,
effort must be made accordingly, and the wielder of the Pināka must be propitiated.' / Then those sons of Manu went where the god Maheśvara was.
They praised Pārvatī and Parameśvara with various hymns. / The two said: 'Enough of this! What can be done now about the agreement?
By giving to us two whatever fruit would come from an aśvamedha performed by Ikṣvāku, / that hero shall without doubt become a kimpuruṣa.'
Saying 'So be it,' all those sons of Vaivasvata departed. / Then, having sacrificed with an aśvamedha, Ilā became a kimpuruṣa.
For one month the hero was a man, and for another month he became a woman again. / Remaining in Budha's abode, Ila became pregnant.
He gave birth to a single son endowed with manifold virtues; / having begotten that son through Budha, Pūru, he went to heaven again.

By the name of Ila, that realm became known as Ilāvṛta at that time;
King Ila, born of the lunar and solar dynasties, was the perpetuator of the dynasty.

Thus Purūravas became the perpetuator of the dynasty of Pūru;
likewise, Ikṣvāku is declared the lord of men of the solar dynasty.
In his condition as a kimpuruṣa, Ila is also called Sudyumna. / Furthermore, Sudyumna had three invincible sons:
Utkala, then Gaya, and likewise the valiant Haritāśva. / Utkala was named after Utkala, and Gayā was Gaya's city.
The southern quarter was assigned to Haritāśva along with the Kurus. / Then, having consecrated his son Purūravas in Pratiṣṭhāna,
eating fruits, he went to enjoy the heavenly continent of Ilāvṛta. / Ikṣvāku, the eldest heir, obtained the central realm.
Nariṣyanta's son was named Śuka, possessed of great strength. / From Nābhāga came Ambarīṣa, and Dhṛṣṭa had three sons:
Dhṛṣṭaketu, then Svadharmā, and the valiant Raṇadhṛṣṭa. / Śaryāti had a son named Ānarta, and Sukanyā was his daughter.
Ānarta had a majestic son, Rocamāna. / Ānarta became the name of the country, and Kuśasthalī was the city.
From Rocamāna came Reva, and from Reva arose Raivata; / his other name was Kakudmin, the eldest of a hundred sons.
His daughter was Revatī, famed as the wife of Balarāma. / And from Karūṣa came the Kārūṣas, many and famous on earth.
Pṛṣadhra became a śūdra by slaying a cow, because of his guru's curse. / Now, among the sons of Ikṣvāku named Vikukṣi, Nimi, and Daṇḍaka,
these were the foremost of a hundred sons, and fifty other sons of his / were born north of Mount Meru, best of earthly kings.
And forty-eight others who were among that hundred / are celebrated as kings to the south of Mount Meru.
From the eldest was born one named Kakutstha; his son was Suyodhana. / His son was named Pṛthu; Viśva was that Pṛthu's son.
Ārdra was his son, and Yuvanāśva came from him. / Yuvanāśva had a valiant son named Śāvasta,
by whom Śāvastī was built in the country of Aṅga, O king! / From Śāvasta came Bṛhadaśva, and Kuvalāśva arose from him.
He attained the title Dhundhumāra after slaying the asura Dhundhu in former times. / Three sons were born to him: Dṛḍhāśva, Ghṛṇi,
and the famous, majestic Kapilāśva, sons of Dhundhumāra. / Pramoda was the son of Dṛḍhāśva, and Haryaśva was his son.
Nikumbha was born to Haryaśva; from him came Saṃhatāśva. / Akṛtāśva and Raṇāśva were both sons of Saṃhatāśva.
Yuvanāśva was Raṇāśva's son, and Māndhātṛ came from him. / Purukutsa was born to Māndhātṛ, and King Dharmasetu,
and the famed, majestic Mucukunda, a friend of Śakra. / Purukutsa had a son, Dussaha, the lord of the Narmadā.
Saṃbhūti was his son, and Tridhanvan came from him. / A son was born to Tridhanvan known as Trayyāruṇa.
His son was named Satyavrata, and from him Satyaratha is remembered. / His son was Hariścandra, and from Hariścandra came Rohita.
From Rohita was born Vṛka; from Vṛka, Bāhu was born. / Sagara was his son, a supremely righteous king.
Sagara had two wives, Prabhā and Bhānumatī. / Formerly, Aurva's fire was propitiated by both of them through desire for sons.
Satisfied, Aurva granted the two an excellent boon as they desired: / sixty thousand sons to one, and a single son to the other.

Prabhā chose the founder of the dynasty and chose many sons;
Bhānumatī chose one son, Asamañjasa.
Then the Yādava princess Prabhā gave birth to sixty thousand sons, / who, while digging the earth in search of the horse, were burnt by Viṣṇu.
Asamañjas had a son celebrated by the name Aṃśumat. / His son was Dilīpa, and from Dilīpa came Bhagīratha,
by whom, having performed austerities, the river Gaṅgā, daughter of Bhagīratha, was brought down. / Bhagīratha's son was famed as Nābhāga.
To Nābhāga was born Ambarīṣa; Sindhudvīpa came from him. / His son was Ayutāyus, and Ṛtuparṇa arose from him.
His son was Kalmāṣapāda; and Sarvakarman is remembered as his son. / His son was Anaraṇya, and Nighna was his son.
Two sons were born to Nighna, Anamitra and Raghu, the best [of men]. / Anamitra went to the forest to destroy his enemies, O king.
From Raghu came Dilīpa, and from Dilīpa likewise Aja. / Dīrghabāhu was born from Aja, and from him came Prajāpāla.
From him Daśaratha was born. His sons were four, / all having the nature of Nārāyaṇa; of them, Rāma was the eldest.
He put an end to Rāvaṇa, and likewise increased the lineage of the Raghus. / Vālmīki, the best of the Bhārgavas, composed his life-story.
His son was named Kuśa, who increased the Ikṣvāku family. / Atithi was born from Kuśa, and Niṣadha was his son.
Nala was born from Niṣadha, and from him Nabhas was born. / From Nabhas came Puṇḍarīka, and after him Kṣemadhanvan.
His son was the heroic Devānīka, possessed of majesty. / Ahīnagu was his son, and Sahasrāśva came after him.
Then came Candrāvaloka, and after him Tārāpīḍa was born. / His son was Candragiri, and Candra was his son.
From him was born Śrutāyus, who was struck down in the Bhārata war. / Two Nalas are celebrated in whose lineage especially:
the son of Vīrasena, and likewise the king of the Niṣadhas. / These were the kings in the solar lineage who gave abundant sacrificial gifts,
born of the Ikṣvāku lineage, who have been proclaimed as the foremost.

1.9.m: Bhīṣma said: / O venerable one, I wish to hear of the excellent lineage of the ancestors, / and especially of the Sun, of the Lord of Śrāddha, and of the Moon.
Pulastya said: / Come, I will tell you of the excellent lineage of the ancestors. / In heaven there are seven classes of ancestors; three of them are formless,
and four are endowed with form, all of immeasurable splendour. / The formless classes of ancestors belong to the Prajāpati Vairāja;
they are celebrated as the Vairājas, whom the hosts of gods worship. / Those who have fallen from yoga attain these eternal worlds.
At the end of a day of Brahmā they are born again as expounders of the Veda. / Attaining once again that memory, and supreme Yoga and Sāṃkhya,
they reach perfection through yoga, from which non-return is hard to attain. / Therefore, śrāddhas must be given by donors only to yogins.
Their mind-born daughter is known to be the wife of Himavat; / Maināka was his heir, and Krauñca was his son,
by whom Krauñcadvīpa is recalled, the fourth [continent], abounding in clarified butter. / Then Menā gave birth to three daughters possessed of yoga:
Umā, Ekaparṇā, and Aparṇā, devoted to severe vows. / One was given to Rudra, one to Bhṛgu, and another to Jaigīṣavya.
The maidens, excelling all the world in ascetic power, were given by Himavat. / I shall tell you of the ancestral world celebrated in song; listen to that.
There are worlds called Somapatha, where the sons of Marīci / dwell—the ancestors whom the gods honour fully.
There the sacrificers known as the Agniṣvāttas reside. / Of them, there was an excellent woman, a daughter named Acchodā.
And there was the lake Acchoda, fashioned in ancient times by the ancestors. / Then Acchodā performed divine tapas for a thousand years.
The ancestors, being pleased, arrived intending to grant her a boon, / all bearing divine forms, with divine garlands and unguents,
all pre-eminent, mighty, resembling Kāma. / Seeing among them the ancestor named Amāvasu, that woman,
seeking a boon, afflicted by Kāma, chose him for union. / But that proud woman fell from yoga due to that transgression;
formerly not touching the earth, she then fell to the surface of the earth. / Likewise, because Amāvasu did not feel desire toward her,
by his steadfastness she became celebrated in the world as Amāvāsyā, / since she is dear to the ancestors and makes what is offered inexhaustible.
Acchodā, downcast, wretched, and ashamed because of the loss of her tapas, / prayed to the ancestors again for her own restoration.
To that ashamed, ascetic woman the ancestors said this, / perceiving the future and also what was the work of the gods at that time.
The noble ones said this in a voice gracious and auspicious: / “Whatever is done by the wise in heaven with a divine body,
the fruit of that action is experienced by that very body, O fair-complexioned one. / Actions bear fruit immediately in godhood, but after death in humanity.
Therefore, having performed good deeds, you will obtain the fruit after death: / In the twenty-eighth Dvāpara age you will be born from a fish’s womb.
Due to transgression against the ancestors, you will reach a painful birth; / nevertheless, you will surely become the daughter of King Vasu.
As a maiden you will again attain those divine worlds that are difficult to reach. / By the semen of Parāśara you will obtain a single son
on an island abundant in jujube trees, Bādarāyaṇa indeed. / That son of yours will divide the single Veda into many.
And you will bear two sons of the Paurava Śaṃtanu, who was a portion of the Ocean: / the prince Vicitravīrya and likewise King Citrāṅgada.
Having produced these two sons born of the wife of that wise king, / you will again become the Prauṣṭhapadī-Aṣṭakā in the world of the ancestors.
Known by the name Satyavatī in the world, and likewise Aṣṭakā in the world of the ancestors, / constantly granting longevity and health, bestowing the fruit of all desires,
you will be in the supreme world; and you will also become a river, / a foremost river of holy waters, known in the worlds as Acchodā.”

Having been addressed thus by those attendants, she vanished right there;
she too obtained the fruit of her misconduct, which was declared by me formerly.
And there are other luminous worlds in heaven named Vibhrāja, / where the ancestors of good vows, the Barhiṣads, reside,
where thousands of aerial chariots are arranged on sacrificial grass, / where wish-granting trees stand, bestowing fruits,
where those who offer śrāddhas rejoice in prosperity-filled mansions; / which the Dānavas, hosts of Asuras, hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases,
and the hosts of Yakṣas and Rākṣasas worship in heaven, as do the deities. / The hundreds of sons of Pulastya, endowed with the power of tapas and yoga,
high-souled and fortunate, grant fearlessness to their devotees. / Their mind-born daughter, celebrated in heaven, is Pīvarī,
a yoginī and mother of yoga, who performed terrible tapas. / The Lord was pleased with her, and she then chose a boon from him:
“Grant me a husband possessed of yoga, handsome, and of conquered senses, / O Lord, if you are pleased with me, O best of speakers.”
The Lord said: “When Vyāsa’s son Śuka will be born, / you will be the wife of that teacher of yoga, O woman of good vows.
And you will have a daughter named Kṛtvī, a yoginī; / she is to be given to the lord of the Pañcālas, and at that time to the Sātvata.
She is remembered as the mother of Brahmadatta, who reached the conclusion of yoga. / And your sons will be Kṛṣṇa, Gaura, and Śambhu.
They are pure even in aerial chariots enriched with every desire; / how much more so the brāhmaṇas who offer śrāddha, full of devotion and engaged in rituals!”
Their mind-born daughter, named Gaur, shines in heaven; / Sukanyā, the beloved wife who increases the fame of the Sādhyas.
The realms named Marīcigarbha are situated in the orb of the sun, / where dwell the ancestors called the Haviṣmats, the sons of Aṅgiras.
The best among kṣatriyas who perform the śrāddha at holy places go there; / indeed, they are the ancestors of kings, bestowing the fruits of heavenly enjoyment.
Their mind-born daughter is famed as Yaśodā, / the noble wife of Aṃśumat and the daughter-in-law of Pañcajana;
and mother of Dilīpa, the grandmother of Bhagīratha. / The realms named Kāmadughā bestow the fruit of desired enjoyments,
where the ancestors named Susvadhās dwell, those sons [of Pulaha]; / in the realms of the ājyapās, [the sons] of the prajāpati Kardama,
who are the heirs of Pulaha's elder brother, the vaiśyas honor them. / There, all performers of śrāddha who have arrived see together
mothers, brothers, fathers, sisters, friends, relations, and kin, / even those seen across myriad births and experienced by the thousands.
Their mind-born daughter is famed by the name Virajā; / she was the wife of Nahuṣa and likewise the mother of Yayāti.
She later became Aṣṭakā and, being chaste, went to the realm of Brahmā. / These three classes have been proclaimed; now I declare the fourth.
The realms named Sumanas are situated above the realm of Brahmā, / where the ancestors named Somapās dwell eternally.
All of them are embodiments of dharma, remembered as superior to Brahmā. / Having attained the nature of Brahman at the end of dissolution, those yogins,
after performing all the creations and other acts, now remain in the mind. / Their daughter is the water-bearing river named Narmadā,
which purifies living beings and flows into the western ocean. / Human beings everywhere, having understood that which was ordained for them
in the creation of offspring, always perform śrāddhas with a disposition toward dharma. / From their grace alone there is always an unbroken succession of yoga.
Thus was the śrāddha ordained for the ancestors at the beginning of creation. / For all of them, a vessel of silver or adorned with silver,
offered after invoking svadhā, always gratifies the ancestors. / The wise should perform the satiation for the Āgnīdhras and Somapās.
In the absence of sacrificial fire, [it should be offered] into the hand of a brāhmaṇa, or into water, / or onto the ear of a goat, the ear of a horse, in a cow-pen, or beside [an image of] Śiva.
The southern direction is praised as the pure region of the ancestors. / The sacred thread worn over the right shoulder, water, and the offering of sesame seeds [are prescribed].
The meat called rhinoceros, and food such as wild millet and winter rice, / barley, wild rice, mung beans, sugarcane, white flowers, and fruits
are dear and always commended for the ancestors in this world; / [likewise] darbha grass, black gram, sixty-day rice, cow's milk, honey, and clarified butter.
I shall also declare the materials that are to be avoided in a śrāddha: / lentils, sunn hemp, niṣpāva beans, rājamāṣa beans, horse gram,
lotus, bilva, arka, dhattūra, pāribhadra, and aṭarūṣaka. / In ancestral rites, the milk of goats and sheep should also not be offered;
kodrava grain, udāra, varaṭa, kapittha fruit, madhuka, and flax seed— / one desiring prosperity must never offer these to the ancestors.
Whoever pleases the ancestors with devotion, they in turn please him; / the ancestors grant nourishment, health of body, and the fruit of offspring.
Moreover, ancestral rites are superior even to rites for the gods; / the satiation of the ancestors is traditional before that of the deities.
Quick to be pleased, free of anger, detached, steadfast in affection, / calm-souled, dedicated to purity, and always speaking kindly,
devoted to their devotees, bestowing joy, the ancestors are deities of the sacred days. / The sun is remembered as the god of the śrāddha in the domain of the Haviṣmats.
Thus all this recitation of the lineage of ancestors has been proclaimed. / It is meritorious, purifying, and healthy, and should always be recited by men.
Bhīṣma said: / Having heard all this, supreme devotion has arisen once more [in me]. / [Tell me of] the proper time for śrāddha, the procedure, and indeed the śrāddha itself,
which twice-born men are to be fed at śrāddhas and which are to be excluded from a śrāddha, / or during which part of the day one should begin the śrāddha for the ancestors;
how the food given in a śrāddha reaches [them], O best of knowers of Brahman; / by what rule it must be performed, and how it pleases those ancestors.
Pulastya said: / One should perform a śrāddha every day with food, with water, / or even with milk, roots, and fruits, bringing joy to the ancestors.
Śrāddha is said to be of three kinds: daily, occasional, and optional. / First I shall describe the daily [śrāddha], which is destitute of arghya and invocation.
One should know it as lacking deities; the pārvaṇa is prescribed on the change-of-moon days. / The pārvaṇa is declared to be threefold; listen with care, O king.
Hear, O ruler of men, of those who are to be employed in the pārvaṇa: / one who maintains the five fires, a snātaka, one who recites the Trisauparṇa, one who knows the six limbs of the Veda,

a śrotriya, the son of a śrotriya, one skilled in the statements of injunctions, / an all-knower, one possessed of the Veda, knowledgeable in mantras, endowed with knowledge, pedigree, and noble birth,
one who has studied the Triṇāciketa, one who knows the Trimadhu, one well-established in the other scriptures, / a knower of the Purāṇas, a knower of Brahman, devoted to personal recitation and japa,
devoted to Brahmā, dedicated to the ancestors, a devotee of the sun, or a Vaiṣṇava, / a brāhmaṇa whose soul is fixed in yoga, who has subdued himself, and is virtuous.
These should be pleased with effort; listen now to those who are to be avoided: / an outcaste, his son, a eunuch, a slanderer, one with a deformed limb, one who is diseased—
all these are indeed to be excluded at the time of a śrāddha by those who perceive righteousness. / Either on the previous day or on the day itself, one should invite the modest ones.
The ancestors approach those invited twice-born men; / having become wind-bodied, they go and attend upon them as they sit.
Touching the right knee and letting down the left, one should invite [them]: / "Free from anger, devoted to purity, well-bathed, and speakers of sacred lore
must you be, as well as I, in this rite of śrāddha." / Having performed the pitṛyajña, one possessing the sacrificial fire, beginning with libation,
should perform the piṇḍānvāhāryaka śrāddha at the waning of the moon. / On a clean spot smeared with cow dung, sloping to the south,
he should begin the śrāddha with devotion, in a cow-pen or near water. / One possessing the sacrificial fire should offer the ancestral caru or barley flour by handfuls,
saying: "I offer to the ancestors," placing everything to the south. / Then, having sprinkled it with clarified butter, he should make three offerings in front.
They should be made a span in length and four finger-breadths wide. / And he should prepare three ladles made of khadira wood, embellished with silver,
a cubit in measure, perfectly smooth, with an excellent tip shaped like a hand; / water-vessels of bronze, a stirring paddle, firewood, and kuśa grass,
sesame vessels, good garments, scent, incense, and unction. / He should bring all this slowly to the south, keeping it on the left.
Having thus assembled all that in the northern interior of the house, / on ground smeared with cow dung and cow urine, in a mandala,
he should wash the feet of the brāhmaṇas with water accompanied by unbroken grains and flowers, / moving from left to right and from right to left, repeatedly bowing to them.
When they are seated upon seats furnished with darbha grass according to the prescribed rule, / having seated the brāhmaṇas who have sipped water, he should address them with mantras.
A wise man should feed two in the rite for the gods and three in the ancestral rite, or one in each; / even if he is wealthy, he should not make an excessive display in this matter.
Then, having first presented arghya and other offerings to the brāhmaṇas for the rite to the gods, / the wise twice-born man, permitted by the brāhmaṇas, should offer into the fire according to rule.
Having performed [the rite] equally according to the rule stated in one's own Gṛhyasūtra at the proper time, / the wise man should then make the satiation with offerings dedicated to Agni and Soma.
That very fire, brought forth into the southern fire, [is used], O best of the twice-born. / Having arranged the sacred thread, then [performing] the sprinkling of water and so forth,

All this must be done by the knowledgeable one with the sacred thread over the right shoulder. / Having obtained [permission], especially from them, he should make the rice balls and water [oblations].
He should give water with water-vessels with the left hand; / he should give everything diligently, endowed with self-control, free from envy.
Having drawn a line with care, he should pour the water for washing; / facing the south, having then placed darbha grass,
Placing each ball one by one, all in order upon the darbha grass, / he should then present them upon the darbha grass with the recitation of their names and lineages.
Having wiped that hand on those darbha grasses for the sake of those who partake of the scrapings, / he should likewise recite the prayer and again offer water for re-washing.
Having bowed with water, through worship with perfume, incense, and so forth, / thus invoking all that with the Vedic mantras as prescribed,
A man with a single fire should pour out the ladle with water alone; / having done so, the wise man should give kuśa grass to the ancestors.
Then he should perform the rites of the balls and so forth: invocation and dismissal; / then, having taken portions in sequence from all the balls,
A man, having first fed those very brāhmaṇas and caused them to sip water, / should serve desired and pure food continually while praising it.
He should avoid yielding to anger, remembering Nārāyaṇa Hari. / Knowing they are satisfied, he should again perform the scattering of food for all castes.
Holding the food with water and sesame, he should throw it on the ground. / When they have sipped water, he should give water again, [accompanied by] flowers and unbroken grains.
He should perform the entire recitation of the Svadhā invocation over the rice ball. / He should make the rite begin and end with the gods; otherwise, the śrāddha will be ruined.
Dismissing the brāhmaṇas, bowing low, having circumambulated them, / looking toward the southern quarter, intending it for the ancestors, the man [prays]:
“May donors increase among us; may the Vedas and our lineage increase; / may faith never depart from us; and may we have much to give.
May food be abundant for us, and may we receive guests; / and may we have supplicants, and may we never beg of anyone.”
This Anvāhārya rite on the new moon day is declared for one maintaining sacred fires. / Just as during the waning of the moon, so it is declared elsewhere as well.
He should give the balls to a cow, a goat, or brāhmaṇas, or cast them into fire or water, / or scatter them at the edge of a mound, or cast them into waters.
He should make his modest wife eat the middle ball [with the mantra]: / “May the ancestors place in me an embryo that promotes male progeny.”
The offering [remains] in place until the brāhmaṇas are dismissed. / Having ceased from the ancestral rite, he should then perform the Vaiśvadeva.
Then, peaceful, he should eat with loved ones what was enjoyed by the ancestors. / Eating again, traveling on a road, riding a conveyance, exertion, sexual intercourse,
One who performs a śrāddha or one who eats at a śrāddha should avoid all of this, / as well as Vedic study, quarreling, and sleeping during the day at all times.
According to this rule, one should offer the śrāddha of the three classes of ancestors here, / whenever the sun is in Virgo, Aquarius, or Taurus, always during the dark fortnights.
Wherever an offering consisting of the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa is to be made, / there it must always be given according to this rule by one maintaining the fires.
Hereafter I shall proclaim what was spoken by Brahmā: / the general śrāddha, as it is called, which grants the fruit of enjoyment and liberation,
On the solstices and the equinoxes, on the new moon, on the solar transitions, / on the new moon day, the aṣṭakās, and on the fifteenth lunar days of the dark fortnight,
Under Ārdrā, Maghā, and Rohiṇī, upon the arrival of suitable materials and brāhmaṇas, / during Gajacchāyā, Vyatīpāta, Viṣṭi, and Vaidhṛti days.
On the third day of Vaiśākha, and on the ninth of Kārtika, / the fifteenth of Māgha, and the thirteenth of Nabhasya (Bhādrapada)—
These are indeed remembered as the beginnings of cosmic ages, beneficial to the ancestral party; / likewise, at the beginning of a Manvantara and so on, a śrāddha should be given by one who knows.
On the ninth of Āśvina, and likewise on the twelfth in Kārtika, / on the third of the month of Caitra, and likewise of Bhādrapada,
On the new moon of Phālguna, and likewise on the eleventh of Pauṣa, / on the tenth of Āṣāḍha, and on the seventh of the month of Māgha,
And on the dark eighth in Śrāvaṇa, and on the full moon of Āṣāḍha, / and the full moons of Kārtika and Phālguna, and the bright fifteenth in Jyeṣṭha—
These indeed are the beginnings of the Manvantaras, which make gifts imperishable. / Even if a man, restrained, should give only water mixed with sesame seeds to the ancestors on these [occasions],
A śrāddha is performed by him for a thousand years; this is a secret that the ancestors declare. / On the full moon of Vaiśākha, on fast days, and likewise at festivals and Mahālaya,
At holy bathing places, temples, cowpens, islands, gardens, and houses, / isolated and smeared [with cow dung], a śrāddha should be given by one who knows.
On the preceding day and the following day, humble in mind, he should invite brāhmaṇas / endowed with good conduct, practice, and virtues, and possessed of youth and handsome appearance:
Two in the rite for the gods, three in the rite for the ancestors, or one in each case; / even if very wealthy, he should not make an extensive display.
Having worshiped the Viśvedevas with barley and flowers, preceded by [offering] seats, / he should fill a pair of vessels placed upon purifying darbha grass.
He should pour water with “Śaṃ no devīḥ...”, and also barley with “Yavo ’si...”. / Having worshiped them with perfume and flowers, he should place them before the Viśvedevas.

Having invoked them with the two mantras beginning with “Viśve devāsaḥ...”, he should scatter barley: / “You are barley, the king of grains, belonging to Varuṇa, mixed with sweetness,

Dispeller of all sins, a purifier praised by the sages.” / Having adorned [them] with perfumes and flowers, he should release the argha water with “Yā divyāḥ...”.
Having worshiped, released perfumes and so on, he should commence the ancestral sacrifice. / Having first made a seat of darbha and so forth, he should also worship three vessels.
Having first made them provided with pavitras, he should pour water with “Śaṃ no devīḥ...”. / He should add sesame seeds with “Tilo ’si...”, and again perfume, flowers, and so forth.
A vessel made of wood, and also one made of leaves, / or he may use one made of silver, as well as one originating in the ocean.
Gold, silver, and copper are said to be the vessels for the ancestors. / Even the mention of silver, or seeing it, or giving it,
By means of silver vessels, or those provided with silver for these ancestors, / even water given with faith serves for imperishability.
Even today, among the ancestral vessels, one provided with silver is for the ancestors, / because it arose from the eye of Śiva; it is excellent and dear to the ancestors.
Having thus prepared the vessels according to what is available, free from envy, / with “Yā divyāḥ...”, he should place darbha in the hand along with the father's name and lineage.
“I will invoke the ancestors”; addressed by them again with “Do so,” / he should invoke the ancestors with the two verses “Uśantas tvā...” and “Ā yantu...”.
Releasing the arghya with “Yā divyāḥ...”, he should then give perfumes and so forth. / Having given an upper cloth preceded by darbha, granting refuge from the beginning,
Placing it in the ancestor's vessel, he should then place it upside down to the north. / Having placed it with “You are a place for the ancestors,” he should serve the food.
There too, free from envy, he should first perform the fire rite. / Bringing it with both hands, he should serve the food,
With “Uśantas tvā...”, [placing] that darbha grass, especially boiled rice in the hand, / along with excellent vegetables and so forth, and likewise various kinds of edible foods.
Food with curds, milk, cow's ghee, and sugar / pleases all the ancestors for a month; so said the lotus-born [Brahmā].
For two months with fish meat, for three months with deer meat, / for four with mutton, and for five with bird meat,
with boar's meat there is the best satisfaction for six months, / for seven with the flesh of the red-goat, and eight with goat meat,
and with spotted deer meat satisfaction lasts for nine months; / and they are satisfied for ten months with the meat of wild boar and buffalo.
With the meat of hare and tortoise, for eleven months indeed; / but for a year with cow's milk or milk-rice porridge.
With the flesh of the wild pig they are satisfied for fifteen months; / with the meat of the rhinoceros the satisfaction lasts twelve years.
With kālaśāka vegetable and with the flesh of the rhinoceros it is eternal; / whatever is mixed with honey—cow's milk, curds, milk-rice porridge—
given [with honey] is inexhaustible; so say the ancestors, the primeval deities. / One should recite the ancestral Vedic recitation and all the Purāṇas,
and various hymns of praise to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, the Sun, and Rudra, / hymns to Indra, the Lord, and Soma, and the Pāvamānī hymns according to one's capacity,
the Bṛhat, the Rathaṃtara, the Jyeṣṭhasāman, and then the Raurava, / likewise the Chapter on Peace, and the Madhubrāhmaṇa,
and likewise the Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa; and whatever else causes pleasure / to the brāhmaṇas and to oneself, all that one should recite.
Recitation of the Mahābhārata should be performed, most dear to the ancestors. / And when the brāhmaṇas have eaten, O king, food, water, and the like,
he should bring food and other things belonging to all the castes with attention, / [and] he should scatter scatter-offerings on the ground in front of those who have eaten:
“May those souls who were burnt by fire, and those unburnt in my family, / be satisfied by what is given on the ground, and satisfied, may they reach the supreme state.
Those who have neither mother, nor father, nor kinsman, nor friend, nor food— / for their satisfaction this food is given on the ground; may it reach them for union wherever they may be.”
For those who died without rites of passage, for the renouncers, for those sharing the family [name], / who have a share in the leftovers, a seat of scattered grass is laid out upon the darbha-grass.
Knowing they are satisfied, he should give water once upon the scattering. / On the surface of the earth smeared with cowdung and cow urine,
placing darbha grass according to rule, with tips pointing south, with effort, / he should offer the piṇḍas according to the rule of all castes, as in the ancestral sacrifice.
Preceded by the preliminary ablution, a man, having spoken the name and lineage, / and having offered flowers and the like, having performed the secondary ablution,

having observed the counter-clockwise manner, thrice circumambulating clockwise with the right hand, / the maternal [rite] should be performed like the paternal [rite], according to rule, with darbha in hand.
The wise man should likewise kindle a lamp and perform the worship with flowers. / Likewise, when they have sipped water, he should sip water and give water once each.
Then flowers and unbroken grains, and inexhaustible water, / with sesame seeds, pronouncing the name and lineage, and he should give the priestly gift according to ability:
cows, land, gold, garments, and auspicious beds; / he should give whatever is pleasing to the brāhmaṇas, to himself, and to his father.
Free from stinginess regarding wealth, he should bring satisfaction to the ancestors. / Then the svadhā-utterance, and water for the Viśvedevas;
having given it, the wise man should receive a blessing from the twice-born: / “May the ancestors be non-terrific”; addressed again by the twice-born: “So may they be!”
“So may the lineage increase!”; and having been answered by them again: “So be it!” / he should perform the svastivācana recitation, lifting up the piṇḍas with devotion.
The remnant of the food should remain until the dismissal of the brāhmaṇas. / Then one should make the household offering; such is the established duty.
The remnant that has fallen to the ground is the share for the straightforward and uncrooked / class of servants; they call that piṇḍa their portion.
This was fashioned long ago by the ancestors as constant nourishment / for those without vows, the childless, and also for women, O ruler of men.
Then, standing before the place, taking up a vessel of water, / and muttering “vaje vāje...”, he should dismiss [the ancestors] with the tip of a kuśa grass.
He should make a circumambulation outside, and follow [them] for eight steps, / together with his relatives, accompanied by his sons and wife.
Having returned, bowed down, and then, knowing the mantras, having applied the fire, / he should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite and the daily bali offering.
Then, at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva rite, with servants, sons, and relatives, / together with the guest, he should eat everything that was served to the ancestors.

Even an uninitiated person should perform this on all the conjunction days; / it is called the common śrāddha, granting the fruit of all desires; / even one bereft of a wife, or even one living abroad, [may perform] this with devotion.
Even a śūdra should perform it without mantras according to this rule, O king. / The third is the celebratory rite, prescribed as the vṛddhiśrāddha,
at a festival, a rite of joy, a sacrament, or an auspicious event such as a sacrifice or wedding. / The mothers are to be worshipped first, the fathers immediately after,
then the maternal grandfathers, O king, and likewise the Viśvedevas, / with clockwise rituals, using curds, unbroken grains, fruits, and water.
Facing east, he should offer the piṇḍas to the former, ancient [ancestors]. / At a celebratory rite, saying “It is accomplished,” he should give water-offering to two by two.
An even number of twice-born men should be honored with garments, ornaments, clothes, and the like; / the work of sesame is to be done with barley, all of it in regular order.
And he should make the eminent twice-born recite all auspicious blessings. / Thus even a śūdra may always perform the common vṛddhiśrāddha

with the mantra of obeisance; the wise one should make gifts. / “Giving gifts is principal for a śūdra,” so said the divine Lord, / because through giving gifts the attainment of all desires comes about for him.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, named the Description of the Common and Celebratory [Śrāddhas], in the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, the first section of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.

1.10.m: Pulastya said: / I shall now speak of the rite for a single deceased person, which was formerly proclaimed by Brahmā, / as it should be performed by sons upon the father's death, and regarding ritual impurity.
A period of ten days is prescribed as corpse-impurity for a brāhmaṇa, / ten and two [twelve] among kṣatriyas, and a fortnight among vaiśyas;
among śūdras a month's impurity is prescribed for sapiṇḍas. / Until the tonsure rite, impurity lasts one night; beyond that, it is traditionally taught as three nights.
At birth also, it is precisely the same across all castes at all times. / Touching of limbs is prescribed after the gathering of the bones.
He should perform the offering of piṇḍas for the departed spirit for twelve days; / that is declared to be his provisions for the journey, for it brings great satisfaction.
Because the departed spirit is led to the city of the departed in twelve days; / for twelve days he watches his son and wife in the house.
Therefore, milk and water should be placed in the open air for ten nights / for the soothing of all burning and the removal of the fatigue of the journey.
Then, on the eleventh day, the man should feed eleven twice-born men, / and at the end of the birth-or-death impurity of the lineage, twice-born men.
On the second day again, he should perform the single-deceased rite in the same manner, / without invocation, without the offering into the fire, and according to rule, without rites to the deities.
One purifying ring, one argha offering, and one piṇḍa is prescribed; / he should say, “May it attend,” and afterward water with sesame should be given.
He should say “Svastī” to the hand of the twice-born, and at the dismissal, “May you take pleasure.” / Those who know the Veda understand that the rest should be done here as before.
According to this rule, he should perform everything month by month; / at the end of the impurity, on the second day, he should give a magnificent bed.
Likewise, having worshipped a golden image of a man accompanied by fruit and garments, / and a twice-born couple adorned with various ornaments,
and having seated them upon the bed, he should then present the honey-mixture (madhuparka) / together with curds and milk in a silver vessel.
Taking the frontal bone [of the deceased], grinding it fine, he should mix it in / and cause the twice-born couple to drink it, endowed with devotion to the ancestors.
This very rule has been observed by the best of twice-born mountaineers; / for that reason, such a bed is defiled and should not be accepted by the best among twice-borns.
If it is indeed accepted, he is fit for a fresh purification; / for in both the Veda and the Purāṇa, [such a gift of] a bed is everywhere censured.
All those who accept it become goers to hell; / a bed woven with gold threads and enjoyed by a couple—
those who unknowingly touch it all become goers to hell. / One must not eat at a new funeral ceremony (navaśrāddha); having eaten, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
It must always be the duty of sons [to act] with devotion to the ancestors; / one should perform the release of a bull, and an auspicious tawny cow should be given,
and a water pot should be given, accompanied by edible foods, delicacies, and fruit, / preceded by water with sesame seeds, for up to a year, O best of men.
Then, when a full year has elapsed, the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite should take place; / for after the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite, the deceased spirit (preta) partakes of the monthly ancestral offerings (pārvaṇa).
Thereupon, for a householder, [it is performed] prior to auspicious rites that foster growth; / one should undertake the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa śrāddha preceded by the deities.
There he should summon the ancestors (pitṛs) and separately indicate the departed spirit; / he should prepare four vessels supplied with fragrant water and sesame seeds.

For the water offering (arghya), he should pour out the vessel of the departed into the vessels of the ancestors; / likewise, devoted to the ancestors, he should then prepare four rice balls (piṇḍas).
With the two [mantras beginning] 'ye samānāḥ,' he should divide the food threefold; / and by this rite, he should cause the water offering to be presented beforehand.
Then he, becoming the fourth, immediately attains the status of an ancestor; / in the midst of the Agniṣvāttas and others, he attains the supreme nectar.
After the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite, nothing is given to him separately; / and the ball of food must be offered only among those ancestors in whom he is established.

From that time forward, at the sun's ingress (saṅkrānti) and at the junctures such as eclipses, / he should perform a śrāddha with three balls of food, but on the day of death, [only] an ekoddiṣṭa rite.
Whoever, casting aside the ekoddiṣṭa, performs [a different rite] on the anniversary of death / would constantly be a killer of his ancestors and likewise a destroyer of his brothers.
That man who performs a pārvaṇa rite on the anniversary of death goes downward; / for when union with the state of heaven is attained, the liberation of the spirit takes place.

Then the performer of the śrāddha, knowing the rules, should perform an uncooked śrāddha (āmaśrāddha); / with that he should make the offering into the fire, and with that alone cast down the balls of food.
When, with the three, the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite will in time be attained / at the confluence of the month, then he is freed from bondage.

Though liberated, he obtains a share of the wipings (lepa) through the cleansing with kuśa grass; / the three beginning with the fourth are recipients of the wipings, [while the first three] are recipients of the rice balls.
The giver of the ball is the seventh among them; thus seven men are sapiṇḍas. / Bhīṣma said: / How should offerings to the gods (havya) and offerings to the ancestors (kavya) be given by men here,
or who usually receives them in the ancestral world, as is proclaimed? / If a twice-born consumes it in the mortal realm, or if it is offered into the fire,
how do the departed spirits, who have the nature of good and bad deeds, consume that food? / Pulastya said: / The fathers have the form of Vasus, and the grandfathers of Rudras,
and the great-grandfathers of Ādityas—such is the Vedic revelation; / the name and gotra of the ancestors deliver the havya and kavya offerings.
The reality of the śrāddha is obtained through devotion and through mantra; / the Agniṣvāttas and others are established in sovereignty over them.
Their names and gotras are their commands even as they take birth; / this offering of worship that has arrived delights living beings.
If by the consequence of his deeds the father, mother, or guru is divine, / his food, having become nectar, follows him even in divinity.
In the state of a Daitya it exists as enjoyment; in the state of a beast, it becomes grass; / the śrāddha food reaches him in the form of wind even if he is in the state of a serpent;
in the state of a Yakṣa it becomes drink; in the state of a Rākṣasa, flesh; / likewise in the state of a Dānava it becomes drink; in the state of a departed spirit, it becomes water mixed with blood;
in the state of a human, it exists as food, drink, and diverse enjoyments; / the capacity for sexual union with a beloved woman belongs to some, and the capacity for digestion belongs to others;
the capacity to give along with wealth, beauty, and freedom from disease— / this is called the flower of the śrāddha; its fruit is union with Brahman.
Long life, sons, wealth, learning, heaven, liberation, and happiness, / and likewise kingship, the hosts of ancestors bestow when pleased, O king.
And it is heard that anciently the sons of Kauśika attained liberation; / through the connection of five births, they reached the supreme state of Brahman.
Bhīṣma said: / How did the heirs of Kauśika attain unexcelled yoga? / How could the destruction of karma occur through the connection of five births?
Pulastya said: / There was a righteous great sage named Kauśika in Kurukṣetra; / learn from me about his sons by name and by deed:
Svasṛpa, Krodhana, Hiṃsra, Piśuna, Kavi, / Vāgduṣṭa, and Pitṛvartin—they were then the disciples of Garga.
When their father passed away, a terrible famine arose among them, / and a great drought that brought terror to all the world.
By Garga's command, those whose wealth was asceticism were guarding his milch-cow in the forest. / [They said:] 'We are sorely afflicted by hunger; let us eat this tawny cow!'

As they were contemplating the sin, the younger brother said quickly:
"If she must indeed be killed, let her be employed in the manner of a śrāddha."
when she is employed in a śrāddha, our sin will surely perish.' / Told 'Do so!' by his brothers, Pitṛvartin, then,
composed in mind, performed the śrāddha, having then made use of her; / assigning two brothers for the gods, and three others in order for the ancestors,
and likewise making one a guest, he, as the giver of the śrāddha himself, / performed the śrāddha with mantras, meditating [on them], devoted to the ancestors.
Then, going fearlessly, they reported to their guru: / 'The cow was slain by a tiger; let this calf be received.'
Thus was that cow eaten by those seven ascetics, / relying on Vedic authority, fearless in a cruel deed.
Then, having perished in the course of time, they became hunters in Daśapura; / imbued with the ancestral spirit, they attained the memory of their previous births.
Knowing dispassion there, abandoning their breaths according to dharma, / unobserved by people, through fasting to death at a holy ford,
the seven were born in the form of deer on Mount Kālañjara; / having attained the yoga of spiritual knowledge, they cast aside that bodily form of theirs.
They died by leaping from a precipice, their minds having developed dispassion; / then those seven yogins were born as cakravāka birds at lake Mānasa:
all by name and deed—Sumanas, Kusuma, Vasu, / Cittadarśin, Sudarśin, Jñātṛ, and Jñānasyapāraga.
Devoted to the eldest, excellent, these seven were purified by yoga; / yet three of them fell from yoga, their minds having become unsteady
upon seeing King Aṇuha radiant and accompanied by women, / sporting with various pleasures, possessing great power and valor.
Born of the Pañcāla lineage, endowed with abundant troops and mounts, / one among those aquatic birds became desirous of kingship.
And the brahmin devoted to his ancestors, performing the śrāddha and affectionate to his ancestors, / having seen the other two ministers endowed with abundant troops and mounts,
the two best of twice-born [birds] desired ministership in this mortal world. / But one became the son of Vibhrāja, known as Brahmadatta.
And the two became sons of ministers, Puṇḍarīka and Subālaka. / Brahmadatta was consecrated in the best city of Kāmpilya,
a valiant king of Pañcāla, performing śrāddhas and affectionate to his ancestors. / Knowing yoga, he then became one who knew the minds of all creatures.
That king's wife then was the daughter of Sudeva, / famous by the name Sannati, who in a former birth was Kapilā.
Because she had been engaged in rites for the ancestors, she became a knower of Brahman. / Together with her, that delight of kings ruled the kingdom.
Once, when the earth-ruler had gone to a garden together with her, / he saw a pair of insects engaged in a lover’s quarrel.
To the female ant whose face was cast downward, the lustful male insect in front of her, / his limbs tormented by the five arrows [of love], spoke with a faltering voice:
"No loving woman like you is found anywhere in the world! / Slender-waisted, broad-hipped, large-mouthed, graceful in movement,
resembling the color of gold, beautiful-faced, sweetly smiling; / your mouth looks as though it loves molasses and sugar.
You eat when I have eaten; you bathe when I have bathed; / you are sorrowful when I am abroad, and trembling with fear when I am angry.
Why, tell me, auspicious one, do you remain constantly with your face cast down?" / Burning with anger, she said to him: "Why do you prattle, you scoundrel?
You ate the powdered sweetmeat leaving me aside! / Passing me by, overcome with passion, you gave it to another woman!"
The male ant said: / "O woman of fair complexion, because she resembled you, I gave it to that other woman. / Therefore, O passionate woman, you ought to forgive this single fault of mine.
I will not do so again; abandon your anger, O woman of beautiful breasts! / Truly, I touch your feet; be gracious to me who am bowed before you.
