If you are angry, O woman of fair hips, death stands before me; / if you are pleased, O lovely-thighed woman, all my wishes are fulfilled.
Drink deeply, O woman of fair hips, my face which resembles the full moon / and tastes like nectar, always devoted to you who have inflamed my desire.
Considering this, O auspicious one, compassion should always be shown to me." / Having heard this speech, she then became pleased.
The female ant surrendered herself for his pleasure. / Having understood all that, Brahmadatta laughed in astonishment,
knowing the cries of all beings through the power of his past karma. / Bhīṣma said: / How did King Brahmadatta become a knower of the sounds of all creatures?
And where did that group of four cakra birds go? / Tell me that, O omniscient one, and in whose family [were born] those of good vows?
Pulastya said: / In that very city were born the cakra birds, O king,
as the heirs of an old twice-born man, wise brahmins who remembered their previous births, / steadfast, seeing reality, endowed with knowledge and asceticism beyond measure.
They were the sons of Sudaridra, [both] by name and by deed. / The minds of those twice-born youths turned toward asceticism.
"We shall attain the supreme perfection," said those best of brahmins. / Hearing that speech of theirs, Sudaridra of great austerities
spoke in a plaintive voice: "What is this, my sons? / This is adharma on your part, sons," said the father to them.
"Abandoning your aged, poor father who dwells in the forest, / where indeed will there be dharma for you, having abandoned me and my livelihood?"
They said: "Your livelihood has been arranged, father; hear our words: / This was formerly a vow [known] to the king; he will give you abundant
wealth and a thousand villages, when you recite at dawn: / 'Those who were brahmins in Kurukṣetra, and hunters in Daśapura,
who became deer in Kālañjara, and cakra birds at lake Mānasa.'" / Having said this to their father, they went to the forest again for asceticism.
That good twice-born old man also went to achieve his purpose, O king. / Formerly, the ruler of Pañcāla was a king of Vibhrāja named Aṇuha.
Desiring a son, he worshipped the lord of the gods, / the lotus-born grandfather [Brahmā], devoted to severe vows.
Then after a long time, the Grandfather, pleased with him, [said]: / "Choose a boon, O king, whatever is desired in your heart; may good fortune be yours."
Aṇuha said: / "Grant me, O lord of gods, a son endowed with great strength and prowess, / a master of all lores, righteous, the best of yogins,
knowing the sounds of all creatures; grant me a yogin as a son." / "So be it," the Supreme Lord, the soul of the universe, said to him,

and vanished right there before the eyes of all beings. / Then his son was born as the glorious Brahmadatta,

He was compassionate toward all living beings, possessed greater strength than all living beings,
knew the cries of all living beings, and was the lord over the lords of all living beings.
Then, through his true nature, he who was yoga-souled came near the ant, / where that pair of insects was resting, enjoying themselves.
Then Sannati, seeing him laughing aloud and deeply astonished, / suspecting something, asked the ruler of men:
Sannati said: / "Why this sudden, excessive laughter, O king? / I do not know the cause of the laughter made by you out of season."
That prince spoke of the conversation of the ants: / "This laughter arose from a passionate lovers’ quarrel, O fair-faced woman.
There is no other reason whatsoever for the laughter, O sweetly smiling one." / The queen did not believe him, and said: "This of yours is a lie!
I alone was laughed at here; I will not live with you now! / How could a mortal, without being a god, understand the talk of ants?
Therefore, it was only me you laughed at today; what else could it be?" / Then the king, left without an answer, wishing to know the truth of the word of Hari,
undertook an observance and remained faultless for seven nights. / At the end of a dream, Brahmā said to him: "Roaming the city at dawn,
from the words of the best of old brahmins your beloved will know everything." / Having said this, Brahmā disappeared, and at dawn the king, going forth from the city
along with his ministers and his wife, saw an old brahmin in front / approaching and reciting.
The brāhmaṇa said: / "Those who were foremost brahmins in Kurujāṅgala, hunters in Daśapura, and deer / on Kālañjara, and seven cakra birds at Mānasa—they dwell here as perfected beings."

Having heard her words, he fell down filled with sorrow;
he attained remembrance of previous births, as did the two sons of the best of ministers.
The composer of the Kāmaśāstra, Bābhravya, was Subālaka, / celebrated throughout the worlds as the Pañcāla, knower of all śāstras.
Puṇḍarīka, too, righteous, a promoter of the Veda and śāstras, / remembering their past births, likewise fell down before him in grief.
"Alas, we have fallen from our actions through desire, through the bondage of karma!" / Having lamented thus repeatedly, those three who had crossed to the far shore of yoga,
in wonder praised the greatness of the śrāddha again and again. / Having given him wealth along with abundant villages,
and having sent away that old brāhmaṇa who was filled with pride in wealth, / the king [summoned] his own son, endowed with the marks of a king,
And the king consecrated him named Viṣvaksena onto the throne. / Then all those best of yogins [went] to the waters of Mānasa;
Brahmadatta and the others, devoted to their ancestors and free from envy, [went] there. / And Sannati became delighted: “I have indeed shown to you,
O king, all the fruit of yoga that is here perceived!” / Praising [her] to her face, the king also said: “So it is!
By your favor alone is all this fruit obtained by me in this way.”
Then, having resorted to yoga, all those forest-dwellers / attained the supreme abode through the aperture of Brahmā by the power of their austerities.
In this way the satisfied ancestors bestow upon men / life, wealth, knowledge, heaven and the pleasures of liberation, a son, and kingship.

And whoever, a wise man, recites this glorification of the ancestors / of Brahmadatta to twice-borns, or listens to or reads [it], O king, / is honored in the world of Brahmā for more than a hundred million cosmic ages.

1.11.m: Bhīṣma said: / In which part of the day should a performer of śrāddha perform a śrāddha? / At which pilgrimage places, O twice-born, does a performed śrāddha yield great fruit?
Pulastya said: / The sacred ford named Puṣkara is indeed regarded as the foremost of all, / standing, as it were, as the fulfilled desire of all the best twice-borns.
What is given, offered in fire, or muttered there surely becomes endless. / It is ever dear to the ancestors and held as supreme by the sages.
Likewise Nandā, then Lalitā, and the auspicious pilgrimage place Māyāpurī, / and likewise Mitra-pada, O king, and after that the excellent Kedāra.
They speak of Gaṅgāsāgara as auspicious, consisting of all pilgrimage places; / likewise the sacred ford Brahmasaras, and the auspicious waters of Śatadru;
and the sacred ford named Naimiṣa, which yields the fruit of all pilgrimage places; / and Gaṅgodbheda on the Gomatī, where the Eternal One manifested;
likewise Yajñavarāha, and the god of gods who bears the trident, / where that golden gift [was made], and Hara of eighteen arms.
Where the felly of the wheel of dharma was shattered in ancient times, / that is this Naimiṣa forest, resorted to by all sacred fords.
And there is the sight of the god of gods, Varāha; / whoever goes there, purified in soul, will go to the city of Nārāyaṇa.
Kokāmukha is a supreme pilgrimage place; Indramārga is also seen; / and furthermore, the sacred ford for the ancestors belongs to Brahmā whose birth was manifest.
Where the grandfather god resides, dwelling in the forest of Puṣkara, / the sight of Viriñci is supreme, bestowing the fruit of liberation.
The sacred place named Kṛta is of great merit, destroying all sins, / where the primordial Nṛsiṃha, Janārdana himself, [resides].
The sacred ford of the Ikṣumatī brings welfare to the ancestors; / the ancestors are perpetually pleased at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā.
Kurukṣetra is of great merit, where the path is seen; / to this day it is a sacred ford for the ancestors, granting the fruits of all desires.
Known as Nīlakaṇṭha is a sacred ford for the ancestors, O lord of men; / likewise the meritorious lake Bhadrasaras, and the lake Mānasa;
likewise Mandākinī, Acchodā, Vipāśā, and Sarasvatī; / likewise Sarvamitrapada, and Vaidyanātha of great fruit;
likewise the meritorious river Kṣiprā, and auspicious Kālañjara; / Tīrthodbheda, Harodbheda, Garbhabheda, Mahālaya;
Bhadreśvara, Viṣṇupada, and the mouth of the Narmadā: / the great sages say these are equal to offering the piṇḍa at Gayā.
These sacred fords for the ancestors take away all sins / even from the memory of men—how much more for those who offer śrāddha!
The sacred ford for the ancestors called [Oṃ]kāra, the Kāverī, Kapilodaka, / and the confluence on the Caṇḍavegā, and likewise Amarakaṇṭaka:
bathing and the like performed there has twice the merit of Kurukṣetra. / Renowned is the sacred ford Śuklatīrtha, and the supreme sacred ford Someśvara;
meritorious, removing all diseases, their fruit is ten million times greater / at a śrāddha, a gift, an oblation, and recitation of the Veda in their presence.
The pleasing incarnation of the god of gods who bears the trident, / named Kāyāvarohaṇa, in an auspicious dwelling of brāhmaṇas,
that came into being is exceedingly meritorious; likewise the river Carmaṇvatī, / Śūlatāpī, and Payoṣṇī, and the confluence of the Payoṣṇī;
Mahauṣadhī, Cāraṇā, flowing at the sacred ford Nāgatīrtha, / the meritorious river Mahāveṇā, and likewise Mahāśāla;
Gomatī, likewise Varuṇā, and the supreme sacred ford Hautāśana, / Bhairava, and Bhṛgutuṅga, and the unsurpassable sacred ford of Gaurī;
the sacred ford named Vaināyaka, unsurpassable Vastreśvara, / likewise the one named Pāpahara, and the meritorious river Vetravatī;
Mahārudra, Mahāliṅga, and the great river Daśārṇā, / Śatarudrā, Śatāhvā, and the city Pitṛpada;
likewise Aṅgāravāhikā, and the two rivers Śoṇa and Gharghara, / and the meritorious river Kālikā, and the auspicious river Pitarā;
these sacred fords for the ancestors are praised for bathing and gifts; / whatever śrāddha is offered at them is remembered as having endless fruit.
The river Śatāvaṭā, Jvālā, and the river Śaradvī, / Dvārakā, and Kṛṣṇatīrtha, and the northern Sarasvatī;
the river named Mālavatī, and also Girikarṇikā, / likewise the sacred ford Dhūtapāpa, and on the southern ocean;
Gokarṇa, and Gajakarṇa, and the auspicious river Cakra, / Śrīśaila, Śākatīrtha, and after that Nārasiṃha;
and Mahendra, and the meritorious, holy Mahānadī: / at these as well, śrāddha is ever remembered as granting endless fruit;
meritorious merely from being seen, they immediately remove sins: / the meritorious river Tuṅgabhadrā, and the one called Cakrarathī;
Bhīmeśvara, Kṛṣṇaveṇā, Kāverī, and the river Añjanā, / the holy river Godāvarī, and excellent Trisaṃdhyāpūrṇa;
the sacred ford named Traiyambaka, bowed to by all sacred fords, / where the formidable Lord himself, the three-eyed god, resides.
Śrāddha offered at all of these becomes ten million times greater; / merely from memory, O king, sins depart a hundredfold.
The holy river Śrīparṇā, the unsurpassable sacred ford of Vyāsa, / likewise the Matsya river, Kārā, and likewise Śivadhārā;
the renowned Bhavatīrtha, and the eternal, holy sacred ford, / likewise holy Rāmeśvara, Veṇāpura, and Alampura;
celebrated Aṅgāraka, Ātmadarśa, Alambuṣa, / likewise Vatsavrāteśvara, and supreme Gokāmukha;
Govardhana, Hariścandra, Puraścandra, Pṛthūdaka, / Sahasrākṣa, Hiraṇyākṣa, and the river Kadalī;
and those bearing [similar] names, and Saumitrisaṅgata, / Indranīla, Mahānāda, and Priyamelaka;
these also are ever praised and superior at a śrāddha, / for the presence of all the gods is recited [as dwelling] in them.
A gift at all these becomes more than a billionfold; / and the holy river Bāhudā, and auspicious Siddhavaṭa;
and the sacred ford Pāśupata, and the river Paryaṭikā: / śrāddha offered at all these is increased a billionfold;
likewise Pañcatīrtha, where the river Godāvarī, / joined with a thousand liṅgas, carries her waters to the right.

That is the supreme sacred ford of Jāmadagnya, an abode of joy,
where the river Godāvarī became perfect out of fear of Pratīka.

It is a sacred ford for offerings to gods and ancestors, attended by groups of Apsarases;
and the performance of śrāddha and gifts [in honor of] fire there is magnified a hundred million times.

Likewise Sahasraliṅga, and the excellent Rāghaveśvara,
and the holy river Sendrakālā, where Śakra went in ancient times;

having slain Namuci, his friend, he attained heaven through austerity.
A śrāddha offered there by men yields infinite fruit.

The sacred ford named Puṣkara indeed, and likewise Śālagrāma,
and the famous Śoṇapāta, where the receptacle of fire [Vaiśvānara] is located;

and the sacred ford Sārasvata, and likewise Svāmitīrtha,
the holy river Malaṃdarā, Kauśikī, and Candrakā;

and Vidarbhā, Vegā, and the east-flowing Payoṣṇī, and another,
Kāverī, Uttarāṅgā, and Mount Jālaṃdhara—

in these sacred fords for śrāddha, a śrāddha attains infinity.
Likewise the sacred ford Lohadaṇḍa, and Citrakūṭa as well;

the divine and everywhere-auspicious bank of the river Gaṅgā,
likewise the sacred ford Kubjāmraka, and the sandbank of Urvaśī;

the sacred ford Saṃsāramocana, and likewise Ṛṇamocana—
in these sacred fords of the ancestors, a śrāddha attains infinity.

Likewise the sacred ford Aṭṭahāsa, and Gautameśvara,
and the sacred ford Vasiṣṭha, and Bhārata beyond that;

Brahmāvarta, Kuśāvarta, and Haṃsatīrtha as well,
and the famous Piṇḍāraka, and Śaṅkhoddhāra as well;

Bhāṇḍeśvara, Bilvaka, and Nīlaparvata,
and the sacred ford Badarī, the lord of lords of all sacred fords;

the sacred ford called Vasudhārā, and Rāmatīrtha as well,
Jayantī, Vijayā, and Śuklatīrtha as well—

those who offer śrāddha in these go to the supreme abode.
The sacred ford named Mātṛgṛha, and Karavīrapura;

the one named Saptagodāvarī, the lord of lords of all sacred fords—
there śrāddha should be offered by those desiring infinite fruit.

In Kīkaṭa, holy Gayā [is situated], and the holy forest Rājagṛha,
the holy hermitage of Cyavana, and the holy river Punahpunā;

the worship of the realms is holy, and the river Punahpunā,
where this verse sung by Brahmā is widely known:

"Many sons should be desired, in case even one goes to Gayā,
or performs a horse sacrifice, or releases a dark bull."

This verse is widely known in sacred fords and shrines;
all men, O king of kings, recite it as they assemble:

"Will some son in our family go to Gayā,
and, having gone, please those seven ancestors before and those after?

This ancient revelation applies even to maternal grandfathers:
which son, having gone to the Gaṅgā, will cast the collection of bones,

or offer a handful of water with seven or eight sesame seeds,
or perform the offering of rice-balls in the triad of forests?

First in the Puṣkara forest, and immediately after in Naimiṣa,
and having reached the Dharmāraṇya again, will offer a śrāddha with devotion?

At Gayā, or at Dharmapṛṣṭha, or at the lake of Brahmā,
or at the Gayāśīrṣa banyan tree, what is offered to the ancestors becomes imperishable.

He who, having performed the ancestral offering while walking, advances along the road,
even leads the ancestors dwelling in hell swiftly to heaven.

In his family, O king of kings, no one becomes a ghost;
and through the offering of rice-balls, one attains the state of liberation from ghosthood.

A single sage, holding a copper vessel with his fingertips, pours water at the roots of mango trees;
the mango trees are watered and the ancestors are satisfied: one action is known to achieve two aims.

No other gift surpasses the offering of rice-balls at Gayā;
satisfied by a single offering of a rice-ball, they go to liberation.

The best among sages call the giving of grain supreme, and likewise the gift of wealth;
what is given by men at the auspicious sacred fords of Gayā, they call supreme, the cause of dharma.

Those who, with complete devotion and delightful mind, having gone to the great mountain and the great river,
behold it at the southern and northern Mānasa [lakes],

having bowed to the foremost twice-born, have attained the fruit of their birth;
whatever a mortal desires, that indeed he obtains without doubt.

This summary of sacred fords has thus been spoken by me in brief;
even the Lord of Speech cannot [recount them] in detail, so how could a human being?

Truth is a sacred ford, compassion is a sacred ford, restraint of the senses is a sacred ford;
even in the home of the classes and stages of life, tranquility is declared to be a sacred ford.

Whatever śrāddha [is offered] in these sacred fords is regarded as multiplied a millionfold;
but whatever śrāddha [is offered] at Gayā, that śrāddha bestows final liberation.

Therefore, a śrāddha is carefully prescribed at a sacred ford.
The morning time lasts three muhūrtas, and the morning grazing time lasts just as long;

midday should be three muhūrtas, and the afternoon comes after that;
evening should be three muhūrtas—one must not perform a śrāddha then.

That period is called demonic, condemned for all rites;
fifteen muhūrtas of the day are always explained [in the texts].

Among them, the eighth muhūrta is known as the kutapa time,
since from midday onward the sun always becomes milder;

therefore, beginning [a rite] at that time is distinguished as yielding infinite fruit.
A rhinoceros-horn vessel, a kutapa blanket, likewise a Nepalese blanket,

gold, kuśa grass, sesame seeds, cattle, and a daughter's son is recorded as the eighth.
Sin is called 'kutsita'; [these eight] cause torment to that [sin]—

because there are these eight, they are known as 'kutapas'.
Beyond the kutapa muhūrta, for a period of four muhūrtas—

a period of five muhūrtas is indeed regarded [as suitable] for reciting the svadhā.
Kuśa grass and black sesame seeds arose from the body of Viṣṇu;

the wise have declared the time and characteristics of a śrāddha.
A handful of water with sesame seeds should be offered at the water's edge by dwellers at sacred fords;

with kuśa in hand, through a single [action] the śrāddha will reach [ancestors] at home.
It is holy, purifying, life-giving, and destructive of all sins.

The recitation of sacred fords and śrāddhas was proclaimed by Brahmā;
a man who listens to or recites it becomes prosperous.

And at the time of śrāddha, it should be recited by dwellers at sacred fords;
it is considered to bring the pacification of all sins and the destruction of misfortune.

This is purifying, the repository of fame, and destructive of great sins,
and honored by Brahmā, the Sun, and Rudra: those who know it proclaim the greatness of śrāddha."

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled 'The Topic of Śrāddha', in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
